subject: religious-studies

items.title: Wittgenstein treated religious language as a 'language game'
items.claim: How did the later Wittgenstein approach religious language?

options.text: He argued religious language is meaningless
Religious language is a 'language game' embedded in a 'form of life' — it has its own grammar, not reducible to scientific assertion; meaningful within its practice
He defended a literal cognitive interpretation
He treated all language games as equally true

items.reveal:
Wittgenstein's 'Philosophical Investigations' (published 1953) replaced the picture theory of meaning from his earlier 'Tractatus' (1921) with a use-theory: 'the meaning of a word is its use in the language'.

Religious language games — prayer, worship, doctrinal assertion — function differently from scientific language games. D. Z. Phillips and Norman Malcolm developed Wittgensteinian philosophy of religion in the 20th century.

Critics (Antony Flew, 'Theology and Falsification' 1950) argued this reduces religious claims to non-cognitive expressions; defenders argue Wittgenstein himself was more nuanced, refusing both literalist and reductionist readings.
items.why: 20th-century philosophy of religion shifted from 'do these claims correspond to reality?' to 'what kind of claims are these?'. Wittgenstein opens space for religious practice without requiring scientific-style verification.

items.title: Vedantic Hinduism teaches the unity of atman and Brahman

options.text: Soul and god are entirely separate

'That thou art' (Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7) — atman (the individual self) is identical with, or in relation to, Brahman (ultimate reality); different Vedanta schools interpret the relationship as non-dual, qualified non-dual, or dualist
Only Brahman is real; atman is illusion with no relation
Brahman is a god subordinate to atman

items.reveal:
The Mahavakyas ('great sayings') include 'tat tvam asi' (Chandogya 6.8.7), 'aham brahmasmi' (Brihadaranyaka 1.4.10), 'ayam atma brahma' (Mandukya 2).

Shankara (8th century CE) developed Advaita Vedanta — non-duality: atman is identical to Brahman; perceived multiplicity is maya (illusion).

Ramanuja (11th-12th century) taught Vishishtadvaita — qualified non-duality: atman is a real attribute of Brahman but distinct. Madhva (13th century) taught Dvaita — full dualism: souls and God are eternally distinct.

All three schools are orthodox Vedantic positions.
items.why: Hindu philosophy of self is sophisticated. Treating Hinduism as 'just polytheism' misses the metaphysical core that has shaped Indian thought for over two millennia.

items.title: Shabbat begins on Friday evening and ends on Saturday night
items.claim: When does the Jewish Sabbath begin and end?

options.text: From sunset on Friday to the appearance of three stars on Saturday night — Jewish days begin at sunset, following Genesis 1's 'and there was evening and there was morning'

items.reveal:
The Genesis creation account marks each day 'there was evening and there was morning'. Jewish days begin at sunset. Shabbat is welcomed with candle lighting (typically 18 minutes before sunset) and Kiddush over wine.

The Torah commands rest from melacha — 39 categories of work derived from activities involved in building the Tabernacle. These include lighting fires, writing, carrying in public, tearing, cooking. Modern applications (electricity, driving, mobile phones) follow rabbinic reasoning by analogy.

Shabbat ends with Havdalah — a brief ceremony with wine, spices and a multi-wick candle marking the separation between holy and ordinary time.
items.why: Religious time is structured differently. Treating Shabbat as 'Saturday' misses both its beginning at sunset and the depth of its observance — one of the most distinctive elements of Jewish practice.
